franks.t: A confederation of Germanic peoples on the lower Rhine whose kings conquered Gaul and founded the realm from which France and Germany both grew.
franks.o: The Franks ('the bold' or 'the free') appear in Roman sources around 250, a grouping of older Rhineland peoples such as the Chamavi, Chattuarii, Bructeri and Sugambri. They raided Gaul by land and sea, while many served as Roman soldiers. In 358 Julian allowed the Salian Franks to settle in Toxandria, in the modern Netherlands and Belgium.
franks.r: The confederation was led by many petty kings, with Salian Franks in the north-west and Rhineland Franks around Cologne. Franks rose high in Roman service, among them the generals Arbogast and Bauto. The grave of King Childeric I at Tournai, found in 1653, shows a ruler wearing both a Roman officer's cloak brooch and Frankish weapons.
franks.e: In 481 Childeric's son Clovis I became king and united the Frankish groups, defeating the Roman ruler Syagrius in 486 and converting to Catholic Christianity. His Merovingian kingdom, Francia, absorbed the Alemanni and Thuringians and passed later to the Carolingians, whose divisions produced East Francia and France.

french-second-republic.t: The short republic of 1848 that introduced universal male suffrage and abolished slavery, then elected the president who would overthrow it.
french-second-republic.o: The February Revolution of 1848 toppled the July Monarchy. A provisional government including the poet Alphonse de Lamartine proclaimed the Republic, introduced universal male suffrage, abolished slavery in the colonies under Victor Schoelcher's decree, and created National Workshops for the unemployed.
french-second-republic.r: The elected assembly was conservative, and the closure of the National Workshops provoked the June Days uprising, crushed by General Cavaignac with thousands killed. In December 1848 Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, nephew of Napoleon, was elected president by a landslide. The assembly then restricted suffrage and passed the Falloux law strengthening Church schools.
french-second-republic.e: Barred from a second term, Louis-Napoléon staged a coup on 2 December 1851, approved by plebiscite. A year later, on 2 December 1852, he proclaimed himself Emperor Napoleon III, founding the Second French Empire.

frisian-freedom.t: A medieval coastal society without lords, in which Frisian farmers governed themselves through elected judges and assemblies for nearly four centuries.
frisian-freedom.o: After the Carolingian counts lost effective control of the North Sea coast in the 11th and 12th centuries, the Frisian lands between the Vlie and the Weser governed themselves. Frisians claimed their liberty came from a privilege granted by Charlemagne, a legend that justified their refusal to accept feudal lords.
frisian-freedom.r: Each land or community chose its own judges, called redjeven or consuls, and delegates of the Seven Sealands met at the Upstalsboom near Aurich. Frisians built dykes and terps, raised cattle and traded by sea, and wrote down their own laws in Old Frisian. There were no knights or castles in the usual sense, but powerful chieftains, the hoofdelingen, rose in the 14th century.
frisian-freedom.e: Feuds between the Schieringers and Vetkopers weakened the Frisians in the 15th century. East Frisia came under the Cirksena counts in 1464, and in 1498 Emperor Maximilian made Albert of Saxony governor of Friesland, ending the freedom west of the Ems and creating the Lordship of Frisia.

french-first-republic.t: The revolutionary republic that executed a king, fought most of Europe, passed through the Terror and the Directory, and ended in Napoleon's empire.
french-first-republic.o: After the storming of the Tuileries in August 1792, a newly elected National Convention abolished the monarchy of the Kingdom of France on 21 September 1792 and proclaimed the Republic. Louis XVI was tried and executed in January 1793, while French armies fought Austria, Prussia and Britain.
french-first-republic.r: Facing war and revolt, the Convention gave power to the Committee of Public Safety under Robespierre; the Terror executed thousands before his fall in July 1794. The Directory governed from 1795 amid corruption and coups. The Republic introduced the metric system, abolished feudal dues and slavery in 1794, and conquered Belgium, the Rhineland and Italy.
french-first-republic.e: Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in the coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 and governed as First Consul, restoring order through the Concordat of 1801 and the Civil Code. In May 1804 the Republic was transformed into the First French Empire.

free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.t: An Alsatian wine town beneath a Hohenstaufen castle that was a free imperial city and Decapolis member until French annexation.
free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.o: The castle of Kaysersberg was built in the 1220s for Frederick II to guard the route from Alsace into Lorraine over the Vosges, and a town grew at its foot. It received imperial-city privileges in 1293 and in 1354 joined the Decapolis, the defensive league of ten Alsatian imperial cities under the emperor's bailiff at Haguenau.
free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.r: Ruled by a council and mayor, Kaysersberg was a modest community of vintners, craftsmen and traders whose wealth came from the wine of the surrounding slopes. The preacher Johann Geiler of Kaysersberg, the most famous pulpit voice of late medieval Strasbourg, grew up there and took his name from the town, which remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.e: Like the other Decapolis cities it came under French protection after 1648, and the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679 completed its incorporation into the Kingdom of France. Albert Schweitzer was born there in 1875. It is now a small town in the Haut-Rhin department.

free-county-of-burgundy.t: Franche-Comté, the imperial county of Burgundy across the Saône, rich in salt and fiercely loyal to its Habsburg rulers until Louis XIV conquered it.
free-county-of-burgundy.o: Otto-William, a grandson of Berengar of Italy, gathered the counties east of the Saône in the 980s and founded the comital house. The county lay in the Kingdom of Arles and so in the Holy Roman Empire, unlike the neighbouring Duchy of Burgundy, which was a French fief.
free-county-of-burgundy.r: Salt springs at Salins and Lons-le-Saunier provided the county's wealth, and a parliament sat at Dole. Countess Beatrice married Frederick Barbarossa in 1156, tying the county to the Hohenstaufen. Through marriage it passed to Philip the Bold in 1384 and joined the Burgundian State, then went with Mary of Burgundy to the Habsburgs and the Spanish crown.
free-county-of-burgundy.e: Louis XIV invaded in 1668 and again in 1674. The Treaty of Nijmegen in 1678 gave the county to the Kingdom of France, which moved its capital to Besançon. Its lasting name, Franche-Comté, recalls its separate past.

frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.t: Merovingian kingdom of the Rhône and Saône valleys, built on the old Kingdom of the Burgundians and ruled from Chalon-sur-Saône.
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.o: The Franks conquered the Kingdom of the Burgundians in 534. At the division of 561 Chlothar I's son Guntram received Burgundy with Orléans, ruling from Chalon-sur-Saône. The kingdom stretched from the Loire to the Alps and the Mediterranean.
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.r: Guntram, a long-reigning king later venerated as a saint, acted as mediator between his feuding brothers' kingdoms. Burgundy kept its Roman law and Gallo-Roman aristocracy and its own mayor of the palace. The Irish monk Columbanus founded Luxeuil there, but was expelled by King Theuderic II and Brunhild.
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.e: After 613 Burgundy was ruled together with Neustria by Chlothar II and his successors, though it kept a separate identity. It passed under Pippinid control, and Charles Martel subdued it in the 730s. With Pippin's accession in 751 it became a region of the Frankish realm.

frentani.t: Oscan-speaking people of the central Adriatic coast, related to the Samnites, who became allies of Rome in 304 BCE.
frentani.o: The Frentani occupied the coastal hills of modern Molise and southern Abruzzo between the Sangro and the Fortore rivers. Ancient writers considered them of Samnite stock, and they spoke Oscan. Their history before Rome is known only from scattered references.
frentani.r: Their main centres included Histonium (Vasto), Anxanum (Lanciano) and Larinum, which some writers treated as a separate people. They farmed, herded and traded along the coast. They usually kept apart from the Samnite League and its wars with Rome.
frentani.e: The Frentani made an alliance with Rome in 304 BCE, at the end of the Second Samnite War, and fought for Rome against Hannibal. They joined the Italian rebels in the Social War of 91–88 BCE, then received citizenship and were absorbed into Roman Italy.

four-macedonian-republics.t: The four self-governing districts into which Rome split the old kingdom of Macedon after Pydna, a short-lived experiment that ended in revolt and annexation.
four-macedonian-republics.o: After defeating Perseus at Pydna in 168 BCE, Rome abolished the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia. In 167 BCE Lucius Aemilius Paullus announced the settlement at Amphipolis: Macedon was to be 'free' but divided into four republics (merides) with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia.
four-macedonian-republics.r: Each republic had elected magistrates and a council, but contact between them was restricted: citizens could not marry or own land across the borders. The Macedonians paid Rome half the taxes they had paid their kings, the royal gold and silver mines were closed until 158 BCE and timber from the royal forests was banned. The first meris struck silver coins showing Artemis.
four-macedonian-republics.e: Resentment and disorder grew. In 149 BCE Andriscus, claiming to be a son of Perseus, reunited Macedon briefly as king. Quintus Caecilius Metellus defeated him in 148 BCE, and Macedonia became a Roman province in 146 BCE, with the Via Egnatia later binding it together.

falerii.t: Chief city of the Faliscans, a people who spoke a language close to Latin but lived within Etruscan culture, destroyed by Rome in 241 BCE.
falerii.o: Falerii, later called Falerii Veteres, stood on a steep tufa plateau at modern Civita Castellana in the Ager Faliscus, between the Tiber and Monte Cimino. It developed from Iron Age settlements of the 9th and 8th centuries BCE. The Faliscans spoke Faliscan, an Italic language closely related to Latin, though their art, cults and politics were tied to Etruria.
falerii.r: Falerii was famous for the cult of Juno Curitis, whose festival Ovid described, and for its temples decorated with fine terracottas. Its workshops produced Faliscan red-figure vases in the 4th century BCE. The city usually allied with Veii against Rome; Roman legend tells how Camillus, besieging it in 394 BCE, sent back a schoolmaster who tried to hand over his pupils, and the Faliscans surrendered in admiration.
falerii.e: After further wars Falerii revolted in 241 BCE, just after the First Punic War, and was crushed within days. Rome destroyed the hilltop city and moved its people to Falerii Novi on open ground about 6 km away, whose walls still stand. The old site was resettled in the Middle Ages as Civita Castellana.

free-state-of-icaria.t: Tiny independent republic declared on the Aegean island of Icaria in 1912 after islanders expelled the Ottoman garrison, lasting months until union with Greece.
free-state-of-icaria.o: Icaria, a mountainous island west of Samos, was under Ottoman rule when Italy's war with the Ottoman Empire weakened Turkish control in the Aegean. On 17 July 1912 the islanders, led by the doctor Ioannis Malachias, rose against the small Ottoman garrison, forced its surrender and proclaimed the Free State of Icaria.
free-state-of-icaria.r: The new state set up a provisional government at Agios Kirykos, adopted its own flag and issued postage stamps. It lacked money, an army and any outside recognition, and the islanders, who lived by farming, herding and emigration, hoped for annexation by Greece rather than lasting independence.
free-state-of-icaria.e: When the First Balkan War began, the Greek navy arrived in November 1912 and the island joined the Kingdom of Greece. The episode lasted about five months and is still commemorated on Icaria every July.

free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.t: A small Allgäu linen town that remained a free imperial city for five centuries, until the German mediatisation of 1802.
free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.o: Leutkirch grew up as the market centre of the Nibelgau in upper Swabia. In 1293 it received the town law of Lindau from King Adolf of Nassau, and it came to rank as a free imperial city answerable only to the emperor, although the imperial bailiwick over the surrounding countryside was often pledged to neighbouring lords.
free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.r: A small council-governed town, Leutkirch lived from weaving linen and from the market of the surrounding farms. It adopted the Reformation in the 1540s, and its Protestant burghers coexisted uneasily with Catholic neighbours such as the local abbeys and the County of Waldburg. It sat in the Swabian Circle and on the Swabian bench of cities at the Imperial Diet.
free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.e: The town suffered repeatedly in the Thirty Years' War. In 1802, as the mediatisation of the imperial cities began, Bavaria occupied it, and in 1810 it passed to the Kingdom of Württemberg. Today it is Leutkirch im Allgäu in Baden-Württemberg.

fib.t: A Pictish province between the Tay and the Forth, the ancestor of the Kingdom of Fife, named in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne.
fib.o: Fib appears among the seven Pictish provinces named after the legendary sons of Cruithne. Its territory corresponded broadly to modern Fife and Kinross, between the Firth of Tay and the Firth of Forth.
fib.r: Nothing is known of its rulers in the Pictish period. The peninsula was fertile, and St Andrews, known earlier as Cennrigmonaid, became one of the leading Pictish churches, receiving relics of Saint Andrew by tradition in the 8th century.
fib.e: Fib became the earldom of Fife within the Kingdom of Scotland, whose earls held the right to enthrone the king at Scone. Fife still calls itself 'the Kingdom'.

fidenae.t: Small town on the Tiber just north of Rome, allied with Veii, which Rome fought for repeatedly and finally destroyed in 426 BCE.
fidenae.o: Fidenae stood on a hill above the left bank of the Tiber, about 8 km north of Rome, opposite the Etruscan city of Veii. It was a Latin town, though Livy says it had Etruscan connections, and settlement there goes back to the early Iron Age. Its position on the river and the Via Salaria made it strategically vital.
fidenae.r: Little is known of its government. Roman tradition tells of repeated wars from the time of Romulus, as Fidenae shifted between Rome and Veii. In 438 BCE it went over to Lars Tolumnius of Veii and killed Roman envoys; the Roman officer Aulus Cornelius Cossus killed Tolumnius in single combat and dedicated his armour as the spolia opima.
fidenae.e: In 426 BCE the dictator Mamercus Aemilius captured and destroyed Fidenae, and its land became Roman. It survived only as a village; under Tiberius, in 27 CE, the collapse of a wooden amphitheatre there reportedly killed thousands, as Tacitus records.

free-imperial-city-of-speyer.t: A Rhineland cathedral city that hosted imperial diets and the Imperial Chamber Court and gave Protestantism its name in 1529.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.o: Speyer, the Roman Noviomagus, was the burial place of the Salian emperors, whose cathedral rose there from 1030. The burghers gradually wrested power from the bishop, helped by Henry V's charter of 1111, and in 1294 the bishop gave up most of his remaining rights, leaving the city self-governing under the emperor alone.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.r: Patricians and later the guilds shared power in the council. The city hosted some fifty imperial diets; at the 1529 diet the Lutheran estates issued the 'protestation' that gave Protestants their name. From 1527 to 1689 the Imperial Chamber Court, the empire's highest court, sat in Speyer. The city turned Lutheran, while the Prince-Bishopric of Speyer kept the cathedral Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.e: In 1689 French troops burned Speyer during the Nine Years' War, and the court moved to Wetzlar. Revolutionary France occupied the city in 1792 and annexed it in 1797. After 1816 it was the capital of the Bavarian Palatinate, and it now lies in Rhineland-Palatinate.

free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.t: Town on the Kinzig founded by Frederick Barbarossa, whose imperial palace hosted the 1180 diet that stripped Henry the Lion of his duchies.
free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.o: Emperor Frederick Barbarossa founded Gelnhausen in 1170 as a market town, granting it privileges and building an imperial palace on an island in the Kinzig river. It lay on the trade road from Frankfurt to Leipzig. In 1180 the palace hosted the imperial diet that issued the Gelnhausen Charter, dividing the lands of Henry the Lion.
free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.r: As an imperial city Gelnhausen was governed by a council of burghers under the emperor's protection, prospering from trade along the road between Frankfurt and the east. Its Marienkirche, with an unusual eastern tower group, and the ruined palace are among the finest Hohenstaufen buildings. The town was too small to defend its autonomy for long once Hohenstaufen power collapsed.
free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.e: In 1349 Emperor Charles IV pledged the city, and it passed to the Counts of Hanau and the Electoral Palatinate, which ruled it jointly. It kept a nominal imperial status until 1803, when it went to Hesse-Kassel. It is now a town in Hesse.

french-ionian-islands.t: Ionian Islands under French rule after the fall of Venice, twice annexed by France between 1797 and 1814 and finally held only at Corfu.
french-ionian-islands.o: Napoleon's destruction of the Republic of Venice in 1797 brought French troops to Corfu. The Treaty of Campo Formio in October 1797 gave France the Venetian Ionian Islands and their mainland outposts, which were organised as three French departments: Corcyre, Ithaque and Mer-Egee.
french-ionian-islands.r: The French burned the Golden Book of the Venetian nobility, planted liberty trees and introduced revolutionary institutions, but their requisitions and anticlericalism alienated many islanders. A Russian-Ottoman expedition under Admiral Ushakov took the islands in 1799, creating the Septinsular Republic. The Treaty of Tilsit in 1807 returned them to France.
french-ionian-islands.e: Britain blockaded and captured most of the islands in 1809-1810, but the French governor General Donzelot held Corfu until it was surrendered in 1814 after Napoleon's abdication. The islands then became the United States of the Ionian Islands under British protection.

free-imperial-city-of-metz.t: A self-governing patrician republic in Lorraine, one of the richest cities of the Empire, which France seized and held against Charles V in 1552.
free-imperial-city-of-metz.o: The citizens of Metz gradually took power from their bishops during the 12th century, and by the late 12th century the city governed itself under the emperor's protection, outside the Prince-Bishopric of Metz. A master-échevin elected each year headed the city government from 1180.
free-imperial-city-of-metz.r: Metz was run by the paraiges, a handful of patrician family associations that monopolised offices. Its merchants and bankers lent money to princes across the region, and the city controlled a sizable rural territory. Metz fought the dukes of Lorraine and withstood a siege by Charles VII and René of Anjou in 1444.
free-imperial-city-of-metz.e: In 1552 Henry II of France occupied Metz under the Treaty of Chambord with German Protestant princes. Charles V besieged it in the winter of 1552–1553 but Francis of Guise held it. Metz became French, which the Peace of Westphalia confirmed in 1648.

french-fourth-republic.t: France's post-war parliamentary republic, unstable in government but launching European integration and rapid economic growth before collapsing over Algeria.
french-fourth-republic.o: After the Provisional Government of the French Republic, voters approved a new constitution in October 1946. It created a strong National Assembly and a weak president; Vincent Auriol was the first. The colonies were reorganised as the French Union.
french-fourth-republic.r: Coalitions changed constantly, with more than twenty governments in twelve years. Yet economic modernisation was rapid, guided by Jean Monnet's planning. Robert Schuman proposed the European Coal and Steel Community in 1950, and France signed the Treaty of Rome in 1957. Defeat at Dien Bien Phu ended the Indochina war in 1954, and Pierre Mendès France negotiated the withdrawal.
french-fourth-republic.e: The Algerian War, begun in 1954, divided the nation. In May 1958 army officers and settlers seized power in Algiers, and parliament called back Charles de Gaulle, who drew up a new constitution creating the French Fifth Republic.

first-portuguese-republic.t: Portugal's first republic, an era of anticlerical reform and chronic instability with some 45 governments in under 16 years.
first-portuguese-republic.o: After the assassination of King Carlos I in 1908, republican sentiment grew in Lisbon. On 5 October 1910 a revolt by soldiers, sailors and Carbonária militants overthrew Manuel II, and a provisional government under Teófilo Braga proclaimed the republic, ending the Kingdom of Portugal.
first-portuguese-republic.r: The Constitution of 1911 created a parliamentary republic. Governments led by Afonso Costa separated Church and state, expelled the Jesuits and legalised divorce. Portugal entered the First World War in 1916 and suffered heavy losses at La Lys in 1918. Strikes, coups, bombings and Sidónio Pais's brief dictatorship of 1917-1918 marked the period, along with the royalist Monarchy of the North.
first-portuguese-republic.e: On 28 May 1926 a military coup led by General Gomes da Costa overthrew the republic and set up the Ditadura Nacional.

free-imperial-city-of-muhlhausen.t: Thuringian imperial city famous as the base of Thomas Müntzer during the Peasants' War and for one of the oldest law books written in German.
free-imperial-city-of-muhlhausen.o: Mühlhausen grew around a royal palace and was favoured by the Hohenstaufen emperors, gaining the status of an imperial city by about 1180. Around 1200 to 1230 its law was set down in the Mühlhausen Reichsrechtsbuch, one of the earliest legal texts in German.
free-imperial-city-of-muhlhausen.r: A council of patricians and later guild representatives ruled the city, which grew rich from cloth, woad and trade, joined the Hanseatic League and allied with Erfurt and Nordhausen in a Thuringian city league. In 1525 the radical preacher Thomas Müntzer made Mühlhausen his base, set up the Eternal League and led its men to defeat at Frankenhausen in the Peasants' War.
free-imperial-city-of-muhlhausen.e: After 1525 the city lost its freedom for two decades under Saxon and Hessian control, regaining imperial status in 1548. It was annexed by Prussia in 1802, belonged to the Kingdom of Westphalia from 1807 to 1813, and then returned to Prussia; it is now in Thuringia.

fidach.t: A Pictish province named in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne, of uncertain location, perhaps around Moray and Ross.
fidach.o: Fidach is known only from medieval lists of the seven Pictish provinces, which named them after legendary sons of Cruithne, the father of the Picts. Its location is not stated, and historians have suggested Moray, Ross or the area around the Moray Firth.
fidach.r: Nothing is known of its rulers, society or government beyond its inclusion in the province lists. It was presumably one of the regional territories of Pictland, subject to the kings of the Picts.
fidach.e: Like the other provinces, it disappeared as a distinct unit when Pictland was absorbed into the Kingdom of Scotland in the 9th and 10th centuries.

free-cities-of-menton-and-roquebrune.t: Two Riviera towns that broke away from Monaco in 1848 over taxes on their lemons and lived as free cities until France bought them.
free-cities-of-menton-and-roquebrune.o: Menton and Roquebrune formed most of the Principality of Monaco's territory and income, through their lemon and olive trade. Resentment at Prince Florestan I's taxes and monopolies boiled over in 1848, and in March the two towns declared themselves free cities under the protection of the Kingdom of Sardinia.
free-cities-of-menton-and-roquebrune.r: The towns governed themselves through elected councils, with Sardinian troops present. A plebiscite favoured union with Sardinia, but it was never formally completed because of diplomatic objections. Their economy remained based on citrus fruit, and Menton began to attract winter visitors.
free-cities-of-menton-and-roquebrune.e: After Sardinia ceded Nice to France in 1860, Menton and Roquebrune voted to join France. In 1861 Prince Charles III of Monaco sold his rights to Napoleon III's Second French Empire for four million francs.

frisian-kingdom.t: Pagan kingdom of the North Sea coast, ruler of the trading port of Dorestad, which resisted the Franks for over a century.
frisian-kingdom.o: After the Roman period the coastal Low Countries were resettled from the 5th century, and by around 600 the Frisians held a realm stretching along the coast from the Zwin to the Weser, later called Magna Frisia. Its first known king, Aldgisl, sheltered the English bishop Wilfrid in 678.
frisian-kingdom.r: The Frisians were seafaring traders whose merchants carried cloth, slaves and goods across the North Sea, and their emporium of Dorestad on the Rhine was one of the busiest ports in north-west Europe. Their silver sceattas circulated widely. King Redbad opposed the Christian mission of Willibrord.
frisian-kingdom.e: Pippin of Herstal defeated Redbad around 690 and took Dorestad and Utrecht, but Redbad recovered much ground before his death in 719. In 734 Charles Martel defeated and killed King Poppo at the Boarn, and Frisia was absorbed into the Kingdom of the Franks.

frankish-kingdom-of-soissons.t: Merovingian kingdom of Chlothar I, who from his base at Soissons gradually reunited all the Frankish lands.
frankish-kingdom-of-soissons.o: When Clovis died in 511, his youngest son Chlothar I received the old Frankish heartland in the north, between the Somme and the Scheldt, ruling from Soissons, the former seat of the Domain of Soissons.
frankish-kingdom-of-soissons.r: Chlothar was the most ruthless of Clovis' sons. In 524 he personally killed two of his young nephews to seize part of the Kingdom of Orléans. He shared in the conquest of the Kingdom of the Burgundians and of Thuringia, where he took the princess Radegund as his wife.
frankish-kingdom-of-soissons.e: Through the deaths of his brothers and nephew, Chlothar inherited Austrasia in 555 and Paris in 558, reuniting the Kingdom of the Franks. He died in 561 and was buried at Saint-Médard in Soissons. His son Chilperic I received Soissons, the core of Neustria.

french-third-republic.t: France's longest-lasting regime since the Revolution, which built secular schools and a colonial empire, won the First World War and fell in 1940.
french-third-republic.o: After Napoleon III's capture at Sedan, Paris proclaimed the Republic on 4 September 1870. Defeat by Prussia, the loss of Alsace-Lorraine and the crushing of the Paris Commune followed. A monarchist assembly could not agree on a king, and the constitutional laws of 1875 created a parliamentary republic almost by default.
french-third-republic.r: Strong parliaments and short-lived cabinets governed. Jules Ferry's laws made primary schooling free, compulsory and secular, and the 1905 law separated church and state. The Dreyfus Affair divided the nation. France built a large empire in Africa and Indochina. It won the First World War under Georges Clemenceau at a cost of 1.4 million dead, and the Popular Front of Léon Blum introduced paid holidays in 1936.
french-third-republic.e: Germany's invasion in May 1940 brought rapid defeat. On 10 July 1940 parliament voted full powers to Marshal Pétain, ending the Republic and creating Vichy France.

free-imperial-city-of-landau.t: A Palatinate wine town that held imperial-city status for four centuries before Louis XIV annexed it and made it a fortress.
free-imperial-city-of-landau.o: Landau received town rights from Count Emich IV of Leiningen in 1274, and in 1291 King Rudolf I granted it the privileges of a free imperial city. In the 1320s Louis the Bavarian pledged the town to the bishops of Speyer, and Landau had to buy back its freedom, which it achieved only in 1511.
free-imperial-city-of-landau.r: A walled market town in the vineyards of the southern Palatinate, Landau was governed by a council and lived from wine, crafts and trade. From 1521 it belonged to the Decapolis, the league of Alsatian imperial cities, and it accepted the Reformation in the 16th century. Its position made it a target in every war along the upper Rhine.
free-imperial-city-of-landau.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 placed the Decapolis under French protection, and in 1680 Louis XIV's Chambers of Reunion annexed Landau outright; Vauban rebuilt it as a great fortress. It passed to the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1816 and is now Landau in der Pfalz in Germany.

felsina.t: The leading Etruscan city of the Po valley, on the site of Bologna, until the Boii Gauls took it in the 4th century BCE.
felsina.o: Felsina grew from the Villanovan villages around modern Bologna, the area that gave the Villanovan culture its name, from the 9th century BCE. In the 6th century BCE it became a city at the centre of an Etruscan expansion north of the Apennines; Pliny called it the chief of Etruria's cities in the region.
felsina.r: Felsina controlled farmland in the Po plain and the passes over the Apennines to Etruria, and traded with the Veneti, the Celts and the Greek port of Spina. Its cemeteries, such as the Certosa, contain the bronze Certosa situla and horseshoe-shaped stone grave stelae carved with journeys to the afterlife. Little is known of its government.
felsina.e: Celtic Boii overran Felsina around the mid-4th century BCE, and the town became Bononia. Rome conquered the Boii and founded the Latin colony of Bononia in 189 BCE, from which modern Bologna descends.

free-france.t: Charles de Gaulle's government-in-exile and armed forces, which kept France in the war against Germany after 1940 and rallied much of the empire.
free-france.o: On 18 June 1940 General Charles de Gaulle, refusing the armistice, broadcast from London on the BBC calling on the French to continue fighting. Britain recognised him as leader of the Free French, and in August 1940 French Equatorial Africa, led by Félix Éboué, joined his cause.
free-france.r: Free France built an army and navy, fought at Bir Hakeim in 1942 and gathered colonies in Africa and the Pacific. A French National Committee was set up in London in 1941. De Gaulle's envoy Jean Moulin united the internal Resistance in 1943. That year the movement moved to Algiers and merged with Henri Giraud's forces in the French Committee of National Liberation.
free-france.e: In June 1944 the committee became the Provisional Government of the French Republic, which returned to Paris after its liberation in August 1944 and restored the Republic.

free-imperial-city-of-selestat.t: An Alsatian imperial city and Decapolis member, famous for its humanist Latin school and the library of Beatus Rhenanus.
free-imperial-city-of-selestat.o: Sélestat grew around a Hohenstaufen palace and the priory of Sainte-Foy on the river Ill. Frederick II made it a town in 1217, and in 1292 King Adolf of Nassau confirmed its liberties as an imperial city, answerable only to the emperor. In 1354 it was a founding member of the Decapolis, the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-selestat.r: A council drawn from the guilds ran the city, which prospered from wine, grain and river trade. In the later 15th century its Latin school became a centre of Rhineland humanism, and the scholar Beatus Rhenanus left his books to the town in 1547; they survive as the Humanist Library. The city remained Catholic during the Reformation.
free-imperial-city-of-selestat.e: Swedish troops took Sélestat in the Thirty Years' War, and after 1648 France claimed the Decapolis. Louis XIV had its walls razed in 1673, and the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1679 confirmed French rule; Vauban later refortified it. It is now a town in the Bas-Rhin department of France.

french-fifth-republic.t: The present French state, founded by de Gaulle in 1958 with a strong presidency, which ended the Algerian War and helped build the European Union.
french-fifth-republic.o: The Algerian crisis of 1958 brought down the French Fourth Republic. Charles de Gaulle returned to power and a new constitution, approved by referendum in September 1958, created a powerful presidency alongside a parliament. De Gaulle became the first president in January 1959.
french-fifth-republic.r: De Gaulle ended the Algerian War with Algerian independence in 1962, introduced direct election of the president that year, built an independent nuclear deterrent and left NATO's integrated command in 1966. The May 1968 protests shook the regime. François Mitterrand's election in 1981 brought the left to power, and periods of cohabitation followed.
french-fifth-republic.e: France remains a secular republic at the centre of the European Union, using the euro since 1999. A 2000 reform cut the presidential term to five years. Emmanuel Macron was elected president in 2017 and re-elected in 2022.

first-hellenic-republic.t: The provisional Greek state of the War of Independence, from the constitution of Epidaurus in 1822 to the arrival of a king in 1832.
first-hellenic-republic.o: In January 1822 the First National Assembly at Epidaurus declared Greek independence and adopted a provisional constitution, uniting the regional governments such as the Peloponnesian Senate. Alexandros Mavrokordatos was elected president of the executive. The new state controlled the Peloponnese, parts of the mainland and many islands.
first-hellenic-republic.r: Divided between notables, islanders and military chiefs, the government fell into civil war in 1823-1825 just as Ibrahim Pasha's Egyptian army invaded. The intervention of Britain, France and Russia at Navarino in 1827 saved the revolution. Ioannis Kapodistrias, elected governor, arrived in 1828 and built a central administration at Nauplia, founding schools and a currency, the phoenix.
first-hellenic-republic.e: The London Protocol of 1830 recognised Greek independence. Kapodistrias was assassinated at Nauplia in October 1831, and chaos followed. In 1832 the great powers chose Otto of Bavaria as king, creating the Kingdom of Greece.

francoist-spain.t: The dictatorship of Francisco Franco, born in the Spanish Civil War and lasting until his death in 1975.
francoist-spain.o: After the military coup of July 1936 against the Second Spanish Republic, the rebel generals named Francisco Franco head of state and Generalísimo at Burgos on 1 October 1936. Backed by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy, his Nationalists won the civil war in April 1939.
francoist-spain.r: Franco ruled through the army, the Church and a single party, FET y de las JONS, with harsh repression, executions and labour camps in the 1940s. Spain stayed out of the Second World War, apart from sending the Blue Division to Russia. Cold War alliance with the United States in 1953 ended isolation, and the Stabilisation Plan of 1959 brought rapid growth, tourism and urbanisation.
francoist-spain.e: In 1969 Franco named Juan Carlos de Borbón as his successor. ETA killed Prime Minister Luis Carrero Blanco in 1973. Franco died on 20 November 1975, and Juan Carlos became king, opening the transition to the democratic Kingdom of Spain.

free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.t: Small Hessian imperial city that became home to the Empire's supreme court in 1689, where the young Goethe trained and found the story of Werther.
free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.o: Wetzlar grew around a collegiate church on the Lahn and received town privileges from Frederick Barbarossa, being treated as an imperial city from about 1180. It lay where trade roads crossed the river, and its cloth and leather trade made it prosperous in the 13th century, when work began on the large collegiate church known as the cathedral.
free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.r: A council under the emperor's protection governed the town, but heavy debts and feuds in the 14th century left it weak, and it relied on neighbouring Hesse and Nassau. Its fortunes revived when the Imperial Chamber Court, the Reichskammergericht, moved there from Speyer in 1689 and stayed until 1806. Lawyers flocked to the town; Goethe worked at the court in 1772, and his stay inspired The Sorrows of Young Werther.
free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.e: In 1803 Wetzlar lost its freedom and was given to Karl Theodor von Dalberg as a county. The Congress of Vienna assigned it to the Kingdom of Prussia in 1815. It is now a town in Hesse known for optics and the Leica camera.

firdafylke.t: Petty kingdom of the western Norwegian fjords of Sunnfjord and Nordfjord, one of the realms conquered by Harald Fairhair.
firdafylke.o: Firdafylke, the land of the fjord districts between Sogn and Møre, is known almost entirely from Snorri Sturluson's sagas. It appears as one of the small coastal kingdoms of western Norway in the century before unification.
firdafylke.r: Little is recorded beyond the sagas. Its people farmed the narrow fjord valleys and fished the coast, and like neighbouring fylki it had its own assembly. Many families from the district later took part in the settlement of Iceland.
firdafylke.e: According to Heimskringla, its king Audbjørn fell fighting Harald Fairhair at the Battle of Solskjel, and the district then passed under Harald's earls. It became part of the Kingdom of Norway and of the Gulating law province.

five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.t: Five fortified Danish towns of the east Midlands, Derby, Leicester, Lincoln, Nottingham and Stamford, that formed the core of Viking rule south of the Humber.
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.o: After the Great Heathen Army partitioned Mercia in 877, Danish warbands settled the east Midlands around fortified centres. Each borough was the base of a jarl and his army, controlling the surrounding district, in an area later known as part of the Danelaw.
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.r: The boroughs were military and trading centres that grew into towns, with Danish law, land units and many Scandinavian place-names in -by and -thorpe. They acted together at times, but there is no evidence of a single ruler. The settlers soon adopted Christianity.
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.e: Aethelflaed of Mercia and Edward the Elder took Derby, Leicester, Nottingham and Stamford between 917 and 920. After a Norse revival from York, Edmund of England recovered the Five Boroughs in 942, an event celebrated in a poem in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. The region kept distinct legal customs into the 11th century.

frisii.t: Germanic people of the North Sea coast who lived on artificial mounds and defied Rome by force and by diplomacy.
frisii.o: The Frisii lived on the coastal marshes of the northern Netherlands between the Rhine and the Ems. To survive floods they built terps, artificial dwelling mounds raised over generations. They became tributaries of Rome after the campaigns of Drusus in 12 BCE.
frisii.r: They paid tribute in ox hides. Roman sources describe no kings but war leaders and envoys; in 58 CE Verritus and Malorix travelled to Rome and boldly took seats among the senators at Pompey's Theatre, winning Nero's admiration.
frisii.e: In 28 CE they revolted against exactions, hanging tax collectors and defeating the Romans at the Baduhenna wood. Rome later abandoned control. In the 4th century rising seas left much of the coast nearly deserted, and the area was resettled, later forming the Frisian Kingdom.

free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.t: The guild-run republic on the Rhine where Gutenberg experimented with printing and Martin Bucer led the Reformation, before Louis XIV annexed it in 1681.
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.o: The burghers of Strasbourg had long resented the rule of their bishops. In 1262 they defeated Bishop Walter of Geroldseck at the battle of Hausbergen and won self-government, and the city soon became a free city of the Holy Roman Empire, outside the Prince-Bishopric of Strasbourg.
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.r: From 1332 the guilds shared power with the patricians in a council and magistracy. Strasbourg traded along the Rhine, finished its cathedral spire in 1439, and hosted Johannes Gutenberg's early work. It adopted the Reformation in the 1520s under Martin Bucer, while Jacob Sturm led its diplomacy and Johannes Sturm founded its Gymnasium. The first printed newspaper appeared there in 1605.
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.e: In 1681, during peacetime, Louis XIV's troops surrounded Strasbourg and forced it to surrender. It kept its Lutheran churches and local institutions, but became part of the Kingdom of France, confirmed by the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697.
